name: Hedonism
era: 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, with heirs ever since
line: Enjoy what is in front of you, and stay its master.

quote.text: It is not abstinence from pleasures that is best, but mastery over them without ever being worsted.
quote.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 2.75, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: The ability to feel at ease in any society.
quotes.source: Asked what he had gained from philosophy; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 2.68, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: He was capable of adapting himself to place, time and person, and of playing his part appropriately under whatever circumstances.
quotes.source: Lives of Eminent Philosophers 2.66, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: It is better to be a beggar than to be uneducated; the one needs money, the others need to be humanized.
quotes.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 2.70, trans. R. D. Hicks

quotes.text: Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.
quotes.source: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation, 1789, chapter 1

quotes.text: To burn always with this hard, gem-like flame, to maintain this ecstasy, is success in life.
quotes.source: Studies in the History of the Renaissance, 1873, Conclusion

quotes.text: The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it.
quotes.source: Lord Henry Wotton in The Picture of Dorian Gray, 1890, chapter 2

words.usage: The one thing good in itself. The Cyrenaics mean pleasure actually felt, in the body first of all.
The one thing bad in itself. Pleasure and pain are the only two measures.
The Cyrenaics held that we know only our own experiences: that I am sweetened or warmed, never what the thing is in itself.
Pleasure and pain are both movements. A state of rest is neither.
The Cyrenaic definition of pleasure, like a gentle swell at sea. Pain is rough motion, like a storm.
For the Cyrenaics the goal is each particular pleasure. Happiness is only the sum, and is wanted for the sake of its parts.
A later writer says Aristippus placed pleasure in the single present moment and gave no weight to memory or hope.
The only time that is ours. The past is gone and the future is unclear.
Time as opportunity. Aristippus was famous for making the best of whatever the moment offered.
Being in control while enjoying. The best rider is the one who can ride the horse, and need not avoid it.
Valued for what it brings. The wise person gets more pleasure and less pain than the fool.
The Cyrenaics, unlike other schools, did not make it the goal. A life is too long and uncertain to aim at.
Pleasure of the mind. Anniceris taught that joy in a friend’s good fortune is worth having for itself.
Pain of the mind. The Cyrenaics thought bodily pains were worse, which is why criminals are punished in the body.
Fine food, perfume and dress. Aristippus enjoyed them openly and said that if luxury were wrong it would not be used at the festivals of the gods.
Turning a remark neatly. Most of what survives of Aristippus is his replies.
The art of getting on with anyone, which Aristippus named as the gain of philosophy.
Saying what one thinks to anyone, tyrants included. He named it as what distinguishes the educated.
Asked what his daughter should be taught, he is said to have answered: to despise excess, and to take heart.
The evening gathering of couches, wine, music, games and talk.
An educated woman who lived independently by her company. Lais of Corinth was the most famous of her day.
The wild plant that made Cyrene rich, used as a seasoning and a medicine. It was harvested to extinction in Roman times.
The school named after the city, not after its founder.
The nickname of Aristippus the Younger, who learned philosophy from his mother Arete.
The nickname of Hegesias, who argued so well that pleasure is out of reach that his lectures were banned.
The nickname of Theodorus, who denied the gods of the city and was expelled from Athens.
The one who does not envy, fall madly in love or fear the gods, though he will still feel pain and fear, which are natural.
From an ode of Horace. The image is of picking fruit when it is ripe.
The Roman word. Cicero uses it when he reports and attacks the Cyrenaic view.

words.meaning: The balance of pleasure over pain
words.usage: Bentham’s term of 1789. He made the greatest happiness of the greatest number the test of law.

practices.name: The first pleasure of the day
practices.instructions: Choose one pleasure of the senses that the morning offers: hot water on your back, the first coffee, sun on your face, fresh bread, stretching. Give it your whole attention for ten minutes. Do nothing else at the same time. Notice where in the body the pleasure is, how it rises and how it fades. When it is over, let it be over.
practices.why: The Cyrenaics taught that pleasure exists only while it is being felt. It is a smooth motion in the present moment, and it cannot be stored. So the skill is to be fully there for it.
variations: Eat one piece of fruit as slowly as you can.
Put on a scent or oil and attend to it.
Lie in the sun for ten minutes with your eyes closed.

practices.name: One pleasure, taken whole
practices.instructions: Plan one real pleasure for today and take it properly. A very good lunch, a swim, an hour of music, a walk somewhere beautiful, time with someone you find delightful. Pay for quality over quantity. While it lasts, do not photograph it, do not check anything, do not apologise for it. Afterwards do not ask whether you deserved it.
practices.why: Aristippus spent freely on good things and was unembarrassed by it. Reproached for paying a high price for a fish, he asked his critic whether he would have bought it for a small coin, and concluded that the difference between them was the love of money and not the love of pleasure.
variations: Share it with one person who will enjoy it as much.
Choose a pleasure you have been denying yourself out of habit.
Spend the same money you would waste on three poor things on one good one.

practices.name: I possess, I am not possessed
practices.instructions: Pick the pleasure that has the most hold on you: the phone, sweet things, a drink, a show, shopping. Enjoy a measured amount of it now, fully. Then stop in the middle, while you still want more, and walk away for the rest of the day. Watch what the wanting does over the next ten minutes. If you cannot stop, you have learned who owns whom.
practices.why: Aristippus kept company with the courtesan Lais and said: I have her, she does not have me. His rule was that the best thing is to master pleasures without being worsted by them, and that going in is no disgrace, only being unable to come out.
variations: Do without that pleasure for a whole day, cheerfully.
Leave a party while it is still good.
Halve the portion and double the attention.

practices.name: At ease anywhere
practices.instructions: Put yourself in company or surroundings that are not your own and make yourself at home there. Talk to someone far richer or far poorer, older or younger than you. Go into a place that is too smart or too rough for you. Dress up or dress down against your habit. Your task is to be the same person, easy and good-humoured, and to enjoy what that place has to offer.
practices.why: Plato is said to have told Aristippus: you alone can wear both a fine cloak and rags. Horace wrote that every condition suited him. He could dine with a tyrant one day and walk away with nothing the next, and enjoy both.
variations: Accept an invitation you would normally refuse.
Make friends with whoever is next to you on a journey.
When something goes wrong today, look for what can be enjoyed in the new situation.

practices.name: Only today
practices.instructions: Go back through the day and mark its motions. List the smooth ones: every moment of real pleasure, however brief. List the rough ones. Then do two things. Drop any regret over a pleasure that has passed, and any worry about one that has not come. And name the single thing you will enjoy first tomorrow.
practices.why: A later writer records his advice: keep your mind on the day, and on the part of the day in which you are acting or thinking, since only the present is ours. He did not toil over the past or labour ahead for the future.
variations: Count how many of today’s pleasures you were actually present for.
Write down one worry and put it away until morning.
End the day with something pleasant and take it to bed.

tasks.name: Cook or order one really good fish dish
Drink one glass of something excellent, slowly
Read the life of Aristippus in Diogenes Laertius, book 2
Listen to Debussy’s Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun, lying down
Accept an invitation you would usually refuse
Journal: what did you enjoy today, and were you there for it?
Is a pleasure in memory still a pleasure?
Say something witty and true to someone powerful
Give up one pleasure today with a light heart
Stand in the sun with your eyes shut for two minutes
Smell the coffee, the bread or the rain before anything else

rules.why: The pleasure in front of you is the only one you can have. Take it with full attention.
Use pleasures and do not be used by them. Be able to stop at any point.

rules.text: Do not toil over yesterday or tomorrow
rules.why: Regret and worry are pains you add for nothing. Only the present is yours.

rules.text: Be at home in every company
rules.why: Adapt to the place, the time and the person, and be the same self in a palace or a ditch.
Say what you think to anyone, with wit and without fear.

rules.text: Prefer the good thing to the many things
rules.why: One fine pleasure well chosen is better than a heap of poor ones.

read.title: Lives of Eminent Philosophers, book 2, chapters 65 to 104
read.creator: Diogenes Laertius
read.why: The main ancient source: a string of sharp replies and stories about Aristippus, followed by a summary of what his school taught.

read.title: Memorabilia, book 2, chapter 1
read.creator: Xenophon
read.why: Socrates argues with Aristippus about whether a life of ease or a life of effort is better, and tells him the story of Heracles at the crossroads.

read.title: The Birth of Hedonism
read.creator: Kurt Lampe
read.why: The only full modern book on the Cyrenaics as a way of life. Scholarly and readable.

read.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
read.creator: Oscar Wilde
read.why: A young man is persuaded to live for sensation alone. The novel that both preaches the new hedonism and shows its price.

read.title: Marius the Epicurean
read.creator: Walter Pater
read.why: A slow, beautiful novel of a Roman youth who passes through a new Cyrenaicism on his way elsewhere.

read.title: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam
read.creator: trans. Edward FitzGerald
read.why: A Victorian poem made from Persian quatrains: wine, a book of verse and the shortness of life.

watch.title: The Taste of Things
watch.creator: Tran Anh Hung
watch.why: A cook and a gourmet in a French country kitchen in 1885. Long scenes of food being made with complete attention.

watch.title: The Great Beauty
watch.creator: Paolo Sorrentino
watch.why: An ageing Roman socialite drifts through parties and palaces, wondering what all the pleasure came to.

watch.title: Big Night
watch.creator: Campbell Scott and Stanley Tucci
watch.why: Two brothers stake their failing restaurant on one perfect dinner.

watch.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
watch.creator: Albert Lewin
watch.why: The classic film of Wilde’s novel, in black and white with the portrait in colour.

listen.title: Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun
listen.creator: Claude Debussy
listen.why: Ten minutes of a faun dozing in the heat. Music that wants nothing except to be heard.

listen.title: Carmina Burana
listen.creator: Carl Orff
listen.why: Medieval students’ songs about spring, the tavern and love, set for huge chorus and orchestra.

listen.title: Getz/Gilberto
listen.creator: Stan Getz and João Gilberto
listen.why: Bossa nova at its most relaxed. The sound of being at ease.

listen.title: Don Giovanni
listen.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte
listen.why: The most charming of libertines pursues pleasure with no thought of tomorrow, until tomorrow arrives.

art.title: Silver coins of Cyrene
art.creator: The mint of Cyrene
art.why: They show the silphium plant, thick-stemmed and leafy, on one side. The best record of a plant that no longer exists. Examples are in the British Museum.

art.title: The Venus of Cyrene
art.creator: Roman copy of a Hellenistic statue
art.why: A headless marble Aphrodite rising from the sea, found at Cyrene in 1913 after a storm and returned by Italy to Libya in 2008.

art.title: Bacchus
art.creator: Caravaggio
art.why: A flushed boy in a toga offers the viewer a shallow glass of wine across a bowl of fruit that is just starting to rot. In the Uffizi, Florence.

art.title: Luncheon of the Boating Party
art.creator: Pierre-Auguste Renoir
art.why: Friends on a restaurant balcony by the Seine after a meal, with wine, fruit, a small dog and sunlight. In the Phillips Collection, Washington.

eat.title: A whole grilled fish
eat.creator: With olive oil, herbs and lemon
eat.why: Fish was the luxury of the Greek table, and half the stories about Aristippus involve him buying one.

eat.title: Roast partridge or other game bird
eat.creator: With a sharp sauce
eat.why: He once paid fifty drachmas for a partridge and defended the price.

eat.title: Honey cakes
eat.creator: Flat cakes of flour, cheese and honey
eat.why: The sweet of the symposium, eaten with nuts and dried fruit when the wine came out.

eat.title: A dish seasoned with asafoetida
eat.creator: Lentils or lamb with a pinch of the resin
eat.why: Silphium is gone. The Romans replaced it with asafoetida from Persia, which is the nearest taste still to be had.

drink.title: An old, good wine
drink.creator: One glass, at the right temperature
drink.why: He drank the best he could get and smelled of perfume. Choose one fine glass over a bottle of something ordinary.

drink.title: Wine cooled with snow
drink.creator: Or simply well chilled
drink.why: A luxury of rich Greek and Sicilian tables, with snow carried down from the mountains and kept in pits.

drink.title: Spring water
drink.creator: Cold, from a good source
drink.why: Mastery includes enjoying water as much as wine when water is what there is.

customs.title: The symposium
customs.creator: An evening on couches
customs.why: Guests bathed, were garlanded and perfumed, ate, and then drank wine mixed with water to music, riddles and conversation.

customs.title: Teaching for a fee
customs.creator: The first Socratic to charge
customs.why: Aristippus took money from his students and sent some to Socrates, who returned it. He said he took it to show them how money should be spent.

customs.title: The ready reply
customs.creator: Wit under pressure
customs.why: When the tyrant Dionysius spat on him he let it pass, saying that fishermen let the sea drench them to catch a small fish.

customs.title: A school passed through a woman
customs.creator: Arete of Cyrene
customs.why: He taught his daughter, who led the school for decades and taught her own son. It is one of very few ancient schools headed by a woman.

games.title: Kottabos
games.creator: Drinking game · Sicily and Greece
games.why: Players reclining on couches flick the last drops of wine from their cups at a small disc balanced on a stand. It began in Sicily, where Aristippus spent years at court.

games.title: Kyboi
games.creator: Dice · Greece
games.why: Three six-sided dice thrown from a cup. The best throw, three sixes, was called Aphrodite.

games.title: Polis
games.creator: Board game · Greece
games.why: The City: a game of many pieces on a grid, in which a piece is taken by being surrounded.

festivals.title: The Anthesteria
festivals.creator: Late winter, in the Athenian month Anthesterion
festivals.why: Three days of Dionysus. The jars of the new wine were opened, and there was a drinking contest.

festivals.title: The City Dionysia
festivals.creator: Early spring, in the month Elaphebolion
festivals.why: The great Athenian festival of processions, wine and new plays, tragedies and comedies alike.

festivals.title: The Karneia
festivals.creator: Late summer
festivals.why: The chief festival of Apollo at Cyrene, brought by its founders from the Dorian homeland, with feasting, music and races.

places.title: Cyrene
places.creator: Shahhat, Jebel Akhdar, Libya
places.why: A Greek city on a green plateau above the sea, with a sanctuary of Apollo, a vast temple of Zeus and a spring. A World Heritage Site. Check current travel advice carefully before planning a visit.

places.title: The British Museum, Cyrene sculptures
places.creator: London, United Kingdom
places.why: Statues and coins brought from Cyrene in the 1860s, including a fine Apollo with a lyre.

places.title: Ortygia
places.creator: Syracuse, Sicily, Italy
places.why: The island fortress of the tyrants at whose table Aristippus dined and joked. The fish market there is still excellent.

places.title: Aegina
places.creator: Saronic Gulf, Greece
places.why: The island where he was living well when Socrates died, an absence Plato records. An easy ferry from Athens, known for pistachios and fish.

places.title: The Ancient Agora
places.creator: Athens, Greece
places.why: Where he first heard Socrates, having sailed from Africa on the strength of a report at the Olympic Games.

ethics.title: Mastery
ethics.text: Pleasure is good and slavery is bad. A person ruled by any pleasure has lost the thing that makes pleasure worth having.
ethics.practice: Name the pleasure you could least easily give up, and give it up for a day.

ethics.title: Presence
ethics.text: The good is felt now or not at all. Hope and memory are too faint to live on.
ethics.practice: Catch yourself three times today saving a pleasure for later, and take it now.

ethics.title: Adaptability
ethics.text: Fortune changes. The wise person is ready to enjoy whatever it brings and to lose whatever it takes.
ethics.practice: When a plan fails today, find the pleasure in what is left.

ethics.title: Frankness
ethics.text: Say what you think without fear. Freedom of speech is the mark of a free mind.
ethics.practice: Tell one polite truth you would normally keep back.

ethics.title: Friendship
ethics.text: The early Cyrenaics valued friends for their use. Anniceris corrected this: one comes to love a friend and will accept pain for them.
ethics.practice: Do something inconvenient for a friend and notice what you feel.

ethics.title: No envy, no superstition
ethics.text: These are pains that rest on empty belief, and the wise are free of them.
ethics.practice: Find one envy in yourself and ask what you imagine the other person has.

philosophy.title: Pleasure is the good
philosophy.text: Every living thing is drawn to pleasure and pushed away by pain, from birth and without teaching. That is the only evidence of value there is.
philosophy.practice: Before each choice today ask plainly: which do I expect to feel better?

philosophy.title: Present pleasure
philosophy.text: The Cyrenaics aimed at the particular pleasure of the moment, where Epicurus aimed at a tranquil lifetime. A life is not something anyone can experience all at once.
philosophy.practice: Is there anything you are doing only for the sake of the whole of your life? Does it please you now?

philosophy.title: Smooth and rough motion
philosophy.text: Pleasure is a gentle movement, pain a harsh one. The mere absence of pain is like sleep, and is not pleasure.
philosophy.practice: Tell apart, once today, feeling good from merely feeling nothing.

philosophy.title: Only experiences are known
philosophy.text: I can be sure that I am tasting sweetness. I cannot be sure the honey is sweet, or that you taste what I taste. We share words, not sensations.
philosophy.practice: Ask someone to describe a taste, and notice how little you can check.

philosophy.title: Bodily pleasure first
philosophy.text: The school rated pleasures of the body above those of the mind, and bodily pain as worse than mental. They are stronger and more certain.
philosophy.practice: What did your body enjoy today that your mind overlooked?

philosophy.title: Wisdom as a means
philosophy.text: Prudence, education and virtue are good because of what they yield. A wise person simply lives more pleasantly than a fool.
philosophy.practice: Which of your virtues actually makes your life more pleasant?

philosophy.title: The pessimist’s turn
philosophy.text: Hegesias took the same premises and concluded that pain so outweighs pleasure that happiness is impossible. The school contained its own refutation.
philosophy.practice: Does more attention to pleasure make you more content, or less?

philosophy.title: The experience machine
philosophy.text: A modern test: if a machine could give you any pleasant experience you chose, for life, would you plug in? Most people say no, and so seem to want more than pleasure.
philosophy.practice: What would you miss inside the machine?

intro: Hedonism is the view that pleasure is the good. It has been held in many forms, in India and China as well as Greece, and it is still argued over. Its first full statement in the West came from a pupil of Socrates named Aristippus, and from the school his daughter and grandson built in their home city of Cyrene.

Cyrene was a Greek colony on the African coast, famous for horses, roses and a medicinal plant called silphium that grew nowhere else and made the city wealthy. Aristippus was born there around 435 BCE. He heard about Socrates from a traveller at the Olympic Games and sailed to Athens to find him. He took from Socrates a way of questioning and a complete freedom from convention, and then drew a conclusion his teacher would not have accepted. If we look honestly at what we and every other animal actually pursue, he said, it is pleasure. That is the good, and pain is the evil.

He lived accordingly, and cheerfully. He charged fees, wore fine clothes and scent, ate well, kept company with a celebrated courtesan and spent years at the court of the tyrants of Syracuse, where he gave as good as he got. What saved this from being mere self-indulgence was a second principle that he stated just as clearly: I possess, I am not possessed. The point is to enjoy without being enslaved, to be able to take a pleasure or leave it, and to be equally oneself in purple or in rags. When he was shipwrecked and lost everything, he is said to have walked up the beach, found the local gymnasium, and talked philosophy until he was fed and clothed.

His daughter Arete took over his teaching and passed it to her son, who gave it system. The Cyrenaics held that pleasure is a smooth motion and pain a rough one; that the present pleasure is the goal, since the past is gone and the future uncertain; that bodily pleasures are keener than mental ones; and that we can be sure only of our own experiences, never of the things that cause them. This last idea is one of the earliest forms of scepticism about the outside world.

The school ended oddly. One later member, Hegesias, reasoned from the same starting point that life contains more pain than pleasure and happiness is impossible. Another, Anniceris, softened the doctrine to make room for friendship, gratitude and love of country. Soon afterwards Epicurus offered a calmer hedonism of few desires and long tranquillity, and the Cyrenaics were absorbed.

The idea returned with force in modern times: in Bentham’s proposal to measure laws by the pleasure and pain they cause, in the aesthetes of the 1890s, and in present-day research on wellbeing. This Onda goes back to the source. It asks you to take real pleasures with full attention, to test who is master, to be at ease in any company and to let the day be enough.
guide.origin: Cyrene, a rich Greek city on the coast of what is now Libya, by way of Athens and Syracuse
guide.era: Aristippus lived from about 435 to 356 BCE. His school lasted about a century and a half

figures.name: Aristippus of Cyrene
figures.bio: Companion of Socrates and the first of his circle to teach for money. Known for luxury, wit and an unshakeable good temper.

figures.name: Arete of Cyrene
figures.bio: His daughter and successor. She is said to have taught for thirty-five years. Nothing she wrote survives.

figures.name: Aristippus the Younger
figures.bio: Her son, called the Mother-taught. He probably gave the school’s doctrine its systematic form.

figures.name: Lais of Corinth
figures.bio: The most sought-after courtesan in Greece. She was Aristippus’s companion for part of each year.

figures.name: Dionysius I of Syracuse
figures.bio: The tyrant at whose court Aristippus lived as a guest and licensed jester. Some of the stories may belong to his son, Dionysius II.

figures.name: Theodorus the Atheist
figures.bio: A Cyrenaic who denied the gods, was tried at Athens and served as an envoy for the first Ptolemy. He made joy and grief of the mind the ends, in place of bodily pleasure.

figures.name: Hegesias of Cyrene
figures.bio: The pessimist of the school. Cicero reports that King Ptolemy forbade him to lecture in Alexandria because listeners were taking their own lives.

figures.name: Anniceris of Cyrene
figures.bio: He restored friendship, family and gratitude to the doctrine, holding that we should share a friend’s pain even at a cost in pleasure.

figures.name: Jeremy Bentham
figures.bio: English reformer who founded utilitarianism on the measurement of pleasure and pain, and applied it to prisons, law and the treatment of animals.

figures.name: Walter Pater
figures.bio: Oxford critic whose call to burn with a hard, gem-like flame made him the unwilling prophet of the aesthetic movement. He later described a new Cyrenaicism in fiction.

history.detail: Settlers from the island of Thera, driven out by drought, establish a city near a spring on the Libyan plateau. It grows rich on grain, horses and silphium.
Into a prosperous family. As a young man he sails to Athens to join the circle of Socrates.
Aristippus is not present. Plato notes in the Phaedo that he was said to be on Aegina.
He lives for long periods at the tyrant’s court, alongside Plato and other visiting philosophers, and becomes the hero of dozens of anecdotes.
After her father’s death she teaches in Cyrene and educates her son.
The followers of Hegesias, Anniceris and Theodorus each take the doctrine in a different direction.
Epicureanism, founded in 306 BCE, takes over the hedonist position. The Cyrenaic school is extinct by about 250 BCE.
The last Greek king leaves the territory to Rome in his will.
Pliny writes that only a single stalk had been found within living memory, and that it was sent to the emperor Nero.
His Lives preserves the anecdotes and the summary of doctrine on which almost all later knowledge depends.
He proposes a calculus of pleasures by intensity, duration, certainty and extent, as the basis of morals and legislation.
Pater’s Renaissance and Wilde’s Dorian Gray make the pursuit of exquisite experience a public scandal and a movement.
The philosopher Robert Nozick proposes his thought experiment in Anarchy, State, and Utopia as an argument that pleasure is not all we value.

concepts.text: The good is what is felt as good.
concepts.detail: Particular pleasures are wanted for themselves. Happiness, the total, is wanted only for the sake of the pleasures that make it up.
Pleasure is a smooth movement of the flesh carried to the senses. Pain is a rough one. Between them is a neutral state that is neither.
Pleasure is exhausted in the moment of its being felt. The memory of past goods and the expectation of future ones do not count as pleasure.

concepts.text: To have and not be had.
concepts.detail: The Cyrenaic sage enjoys fully and is never captured. This is what separates the school from mere indulgence.
We have certain knowledge of how we are affected, and none of external objects. The Cyrenaics even coined verbs for it: I am sweetened, I am reddened.
Bodily pleasures are far better than those of the soul, and bodily pains far worse. Not every mental pleasure even depends on a bodily one.
Nothing is just, fine or base by nature. The sensible person nonetheless avoids wrongdoing because of the penalties and the bad name.
The body is full of suffering and fortune defeats our hopes. The wise aim only to live without pain and distress, and are indifferent between life and death.
A method for adding up the pleasures and pains an action will cause to everyone affected. The ancestor of modern cost-benefit thinking.

facts.text: Not one line written by any Cyrenaic survives. Everything known comes from later reporters, some of them hostile.
Aristippus is the first person recorded as saying that a philosopher is better off than other people because, if all laws were repealed, he would go on living as before.
The silphium trade was so central to Cyrene that the plant appears on nearly all its coins for three hundred years.
The heart shape may derive from the silphium seed pod as shown on Cyrenaic coins. This is a guess, though a popular one.
Bentham asked for his body to be preserved after death. It sits, dressed, in a cabinet at University College London.
Psychologists use the phrase hedonic treadmill for the way people return to the same level of contentment after gains and losses.

glossary.meaning: A member of the circle of Socrates, or a school descended from one

sensitivity.note: Hedonism here means the Cyrenaic discipline of enjoying fully while staying free. It is not a licence for excess. The practices ask for attention and self-command, and none of them requires alcohol or expense.
requiredCaveats: If a pleasure has become a dependence, the mastery exercises are no substitute for proper help.
The pessimism of Hegesias is reported here as history. If you are in distress, speak to someone you trust or to a helpline.
Aristippus lived at the expense of tyrants and in a society that kept slaves. His ease had a price that others paid.
